sentences.text: Eotriceratops was a large herbivorous dinosaur belonging to the family Ceratopsidae and the broader group Ornithischia.
It is classified within the subfamily Chasmosaurinae and the tribe Triceratopsini.
The holotype skull was estimated to be around 3 meters long and featured a short frill.
Its maxilla bore at least thirty-five tooth positions, and the squamosal bone displayed at least five episquamosals and five epoccipitals.
Forward-curving eye horns, estimated at 80 centimeters in length, projected from the skull.
This animal measured between 8.5 and 9 meters in length with a body mass of 11 metric tons, though other estimates suggest a total length up to 12 meters.
Fossil evidence reveals three bite marks above the eye, interpreted as traces of scavenging behavior.
Eotriceratops is very similar to Triceratops but is 2 million years older, more primitive, and also large in size.
Barnum Brown discovered the skeleton in August 1910 in southern Alberta, Canada, but neglected it at the time.
The fossils were found at Dry Island Buffalo Jump Provincial Park, between coal seams, leading to the species name xerinsularis, meaning "of the dry island."
The genus Eotriceratops was formally named and described by Xiao-Chun Wu, Donald B. Brinkman, David A. Eberth, and Dennis R. Braman in 2007.
The holotype specimen RTMP 2002.57.5 consists of a partial skeleton with a skull but lacks the lower jaws.
As a herbivore, Eotriceratops likely fed on plants.
Cladistic analysis suggests Eotriceratops was a close relative and sister species to Triceratops, Nedoceratops, and Torosaurus.
Due to its older age, the authors considered Eotriceratops to be more basal, or lower on the evolutionary tree, than Triceratops, Nedoceratops, and Torosaurus.
The holotype specimen lived about 68.8 million years ago during the early Maastrichtian stage, with other dating placing it between 67.6 and 68 million years ago.
Eotriceratops is older than any other Triceratops-group ceratopsid, filling a biostratigraphic gap between early and late Maastrichtian stages.

Researchers debate whether Eotriceratops is the sister species of Triceratops or a more basal ancestor to it due to its greater age. In 2010, Gregory S. Paul renamed the species Triceratops xerinsularis, but this change was not adopted by other researchers.
